items.title: Xinhua world news summary at 0030 GMT, Nov. 27
text: MEXICO CITY -- Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum reaffirmed Mexico's solidarity with Cuba on Thursday, voiced opposition to any trade or energy blockades imposed on the Caribbean island, and defended the Cuban people's right to determine their own destiny.

During her daily press conference, the president stressed that Mexico's foreign policy is rooted in respect for the self-determination of peoples, and stated that no country should intervene in Cuba's internal affairs. (Mexico-Cuba)

WASHINGTON -- A powerful storm swept across the U.S. East Coast on Thursday, Thanksgiving Day, triggering flood warnings, causing flight delays and leaving more than 800,000 people without electricity.
High-wind and flood warnings were in effect from Virginia Beach to New York City, while Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington, D.C. also experienced severe weather. (US-Storm)
MINSK -- Russia and Ukraine exchanged the bodies of fallen military personnel at the Nova Guta border crossing between Belarus and Ukraine on Thursday, BelTA news agency reported.
The Russian side handed over 250 bodies to Ukraine, while Ukraine transferred 22 bodies to Russia, according to the report. (Belarus-Russia-Ukraine-Bodies)

HELSINKI -- Finland will extend its Border Security Act through the end of 2028, and its land border crossings with Russia will remain closed until further notice, the Ministry of Interior said Thursday.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb is expected to approve the two-year extension on Friday after parliament passed it on Nov. 18. The extension will take effect on Dec. 1, with the law's provisions unchanged, according to a press release issued by the ministry. (Finland-Border)  ■

items.title: Roundup: Eurozone countries agree to nominate Spain's Hernandez de Cos as next ECB president
text: BRUSSELS, Nov. 26 (Xinhua) -- Eurozone member states have agreed to recommend Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB), European Council President Antonio Costa said Thursday.
The member states also agreed to recommend France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier as members of the ECB's Executive Board, Costa said in a post on social media platform X.
Costa said he would propose that the European Council launch consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council.
"This will pave the way for the formal appointment of the new ECB leadership by the European Council in December," he said.
French President Emmanuel Macron also welcomed the agreement on the three candidates in a post on X, describing them as a balanced team that would serve the stability and prosperity of the eurozone.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez welcomed the prospect of a Spaniard leading the ECB, saying that Spain was playing a greater leadership role in Europe than ever before, according to Spanish media reports.

Spain's Economy Ministry said Hernandez de Cos' experience, independence and ability to engage in dialogue would help the ECB navigate a complex economic environment marked by uncertainty and volatility, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
On Nov. 6, Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis announced that Hernandez de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot, former governor of the Dutch central bank had been nominated for the ECB presidency.
Hernandez de Cos has served as general manager of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) since July 2025. He was governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024.
Lagarde, who took office in November 2019, is due to step down on Feb. 7, 2027, nearly nine months before the scheduled end of her eight-year term.

The appointment process comes amid a broader leadership reshuffle at the ECB, with two other members of its six-member Executive Board, Isabel Schnabel and Philip Lane, also due to leave office in the first half of 2027.

Under EU rules, the ECB president is appointed by the European Council on a recommendation from the Council of the EU, following consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council. The president serves a non-renewable eight-year term.
The leadership transition comes at a challenging time for the eurozone economy, as rising energy prices fuel inflationary pressures and pose downside risks to economic growth.

In its autumn economic forecast released on Nov. 17, the European Commission projected eurozone economic growth of 1.2 percent in both 2026 and 2027, with inflation expected to reach 3.2 percent and 3.1 percent, respectively, well above the ECB's medium-term target of 2 percent.
The ECB kept its key interest rates unchanged on Oct. 29, following two rate increases in June and September, leaving its benchmark deposit facility rate at 2.5 percent.  ■

items.title: Xinhua Asia-Pacific news summary at 1600 GMT, Nov. 26
text: SEOUL -- South Korea's top court on Thursday upheld the acquittal of former President Yoon Suk-yeol on perjury charges during the insurrection trial of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo.

The Supreme Court finalized the acquittal and dismissed an appeal filed by the team of Cho Eun-suk, an independent counsel who led investigations into Yoon's insurrection and other charges. (South Korea-Politics-Court)

KATHMANDU -- The Nepali government, in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), launched a project worth 49.94 million U.S. dollars on Wednesday to protect vulnerable Himalayan communities from glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs).

The GLOF-Sanjibani Project, which will run from 2026 to 2033, aims to reduce the risks posed by GLOFs through lowering water levels in high-altitude glacial lakes, strengthening early warning systems and developing protective infrastructure in downstream areas, UNDP said in a statement. (Nepal-UN-Himalayas)

TOKYO -- Japan's Defense Ministry will transport the Ground Self-Defense Force's (GSDF) long-range missile launchers and other equipment that can be used for the so-called counterstrike capabilities to Camp Kamifurano in Hokkaido as early as December, and a new unit will be established immediately afterward to begin the deployment, public broadcaster NHK reported Wednesday.
The equipment to be transported to Hokkaido includes launchers for the GSDF's Type-25 hypervelocity gliding projectiles. (Japan-Military-Missile)
JAKARTA -- Thirteen miners were found dead inside a flooded mining pit in Indonesia's West Java province on Thursday, with 13 others still missing underground, local authorities said.

Rescue teams have been pumping water from the shaft, estimated to be about 100 meters deep, since Wednesday morning. But their efforts were hampered by high water levels, narrow access, slippery terrain and limited lighting. (Indonesia-Accident-Mine)  ■

One of the vessels was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, which was abandoned burning following the incident, the navy said in a statement on the IRGC's official news outlet Sepah News. (Iran-Hormuz Strait-Vessels)

items.title: China urges non-regional countries to stop meddling in South China Sea issue: spokesperson
text: BEIJING, Nov. 26 (Xinhua) -- China on Thursday urged certain non-regional countries to respect its sovereignty and rights and interests and stop interfering in the South China Sea issue.

The Philippines and Australia recently signed a defense cooperation agreement, which the Philippine side claimed would bolster the Philippines' credible deterrent posture in the South China Sea to counter China's actions.

Asked to make comment at a regular press conference on Thursday, Chen Xi, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of National Defense, said certain Filipino politicians, driven by personal interests, have been spreading false narratives about China, stirring up trouble, and seeking to rope in outside forces to back them up and make waves.
Such moves will only escalate tensions and undermine regional stability, Chen said.
"The South China Sea should be a sea of peace, friendship and cooperation. Stoking troubles and provoking confrontation are not welcome here," he said.
The spokesperson urged relevant non-regional countries to earnestly respect China's sovereignty and rights and interests in the South China Sea and cease meddling in the issue.

China's actions to safeguard its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests are legitimate and justified, Chen said, adding that China will continue to take necessary measures to respond firmly to provocations and infringement activities.
China will resolutely thwart any attempt to destabilize the South China Sea, Chen said.  ■

China delivers successful APEC 2026 host year, says Vietnamese official
text: HANOI, Nov. 27 (Xinhua) -- China worked with other APEC members to make its APEC 2026 host year a great success, Vietnamese Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Nguyen Minh Vu said at an international press conference in Hanoi on Friday.

Building on the achievements and outcomes of APEC 2026, Vietnam will promote regional cooperation when it hosts the forum in 2027, with priorities including digital trade, economic resilience, digital literacy, supply chain cooperation and food security, Vu said.

He highlighted the APEC Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework (2027-2030), adopted by APEC leaders in Shenzhen in November, saying Vietnam will prioritize applying digital technologies to trade to reduce transaction costs, modernize customs, expand e-documentation and improve interoperability among digital trade systems of APEC economies.

Furthermore, Vietnam will build on the APEC Roadmap for Innovative, Competitive and Resilient Services (2026-2035), adopted during the 2026 leaders' week, to strengthen the competitiveness of the services sector and facilitate cross-border services trade, he added.

items.title: China Film Festival opens in Singapore with 7 Chinese film premieres
text: Singapore Film Society Chairman Kenneth Tan delivers a speech at the China Film Festival 2026 in Singapore, on Nov. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Then Chih Wey)

SINGAPORE, Nov. 26 (Xinhua) -- The China Film Festival 2026 in Singapore opened on Thursday, featuring seven Chinese films making their Singapore premieres, with a China-Singapore co-production serving as its closing film.
Speaking before the opening screening, Chinese Ambassador to Singapore Cao Zhongming said film serves as an important bridge connecting the peoples of China and Singapore.

Cao said the festival was being held in mainstream commercial cinemas for the first time, with tickets available to the public, and expressed hope that this would draw more local audiences to cinemas to experience the stories.

Singapore Film Society Chairman Kenneth Tan said the seven Chinese films featured in the festival span a range of genres, including martial arts and animation. He said he believed the diverse lineup would resonate with local audiences.
The festival, running through Sunday, is jointly organized by the China Film Archive, the Singapore Film Society and the China Enterprises Association (Singapore).

items.title: Explainer: How is China exploring space together with the world?
text: This image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on Nov. 25, 2026 shows a group picture of the crew of Shenzhou-23 and Shenzhou-24 spaceships. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)

BEIJING, Nov. 26 (Xinhua) -- From welcoming foreign astronauts aboard its space station to sharing lunar samples with scientists worldwide and providing satellite services across borders, China is steadily expanding international cooperation in space.

As its space program advances, China is making international collaboration an increasingly integral part of its efforts, creating more opportunities for countries to participate in space missions, share scientific resources and benefit from the peaceful use of space.
This image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on Nov. 25, 2026 shows the crew of Shenzhou-24 entering China's Tiangong space station. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang)

On Wednesday, Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali joined Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi aboard the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft, which lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China's Gobi Desert.

The spacecraft docked with the Tiangong space station at 11:56 a.m. Beijing time (0356 GMT) on Wednesday, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). Ali thus became the first foreign astronaut to board the Chinese space station and the first Pakistani to travel into space.

His participation in the mission followed an agreement on astronaut selection and training signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025, marking a new stage in bilateral space cooperation that has evolved from satellite development to crewed spaceflight.

According to a CMSA spokesperson, four China-Pakistan cooperative projects in biotechnology and materials will be carried out during the mission. Ali will also conduct an in-orbit experiment involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria.
On the significance of the mission, Ali said, "Now it is time to show this great achievement in orbit and send the world a message that we work hand in hand for the peaceful utilization of space."

Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari said the historic cooperation demonstrated China's remarkable progress in space science and technology, its firm commitment to the peaceful use of outer space, and the significance of building a community with a shared future for humanity.
A man takes photo of a lunar sample collected from the far side of the Moon by China's Chang'e-6 mission, in Vienna, Austria, Sept. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/He Canling)
International cooperation in China's space program extends beyond crewed missions to lunar exploration, where foreign partners are increasingly involved in both scientific missions and research.

Chang'e-4 and Chang'e-6 each carried four international payloads. The Chang'e-7 mission is set to carry six international scientific instruments developed by six countries and one international organization, while Chang'e-8 is expected to carry payloads involving 11 countries and regions and one international organization.

items.title: Tales of Border Towns | Grassland Finery
What does "China Haul" reveal about China?
text: Foreign visitors learn about a pocket-sized gimbal camera at a retail store of Chinese drone maker DJI in Pudong New Area, east China's Shanghai. (Photo/Wang Chu)
A trend known as "China Haul" has recently been gaining momentum across global social media platforms.

Foreign social media users have been enthusiastically sharing their shopping experiences in China, with many saying they plan to bring larger or additional suitcases on their next trips, while others mention that they buy novel products every time they vacation in China.
Smart products made in China, from children's smartwatches to virtual reality (VR) headsets, have become popular topics of discussion.

As online buzz continues to grow, visitor numbers are also on the rise. The latest figures from China's National Immigration Administration show that China recorded more than 11.6 million inbound visits by foreign nationals in the third quarter this year, up 15.6 percent year on year. Of these, over 8.99 million were visa-free entries, accounting for 77.5 percent of the total, a year-on-year increase of 24.1 percent.
Behind the "China Haul" phenomenon lies a deeper shift in how the world views Chinese products.
Technology wins hearts through innovation

Foreign influencers' unboxing lists feature not only Guochao (China chic) garments and accessories from Chinese sportswear brands such as Li-Ning and Anta, but also what have become popular Chinese tech specialties, including DJI drones, Insta360 action cameras, and Huawei foldable smartphones.
Immersive experiences with cutting-edge technology are also emerging as a new draw for inbound tourists.

At a 3D-printing flagship store in Nanshan district, Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong province, visitors can scan a QR code to start a personalized 3D-printing experience. In Huaqiangbei, a major electronics hub in Shenzhen, they can browse an array of advanced products, including artificial intelligence (AI)-powered glasses and companion robots.
Tours of smart factories, meanwhile, are becoming increasingly popular, giving visitors a close-up look at China's advanced manufacturing capabilities.
The growing popularity of Chinese tech products reflects foreign visitors' growing recognition of China's innovation capabilities.

Insta360, a Chinese camera and imaging technology company headquartered in Shenzhen, has shipped more than 10 million cameras worldwide. Its first flagship store in New York City attracted more than 1,000 visitors on its first day of operation.

Chinese drone maker DJI has long maintained a leading position in the global consumer drone market with a market share of more than 70 percent, and continues to dominate major markets in North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region.
Chinese tech giant Huawei's foldable smartphones have recorded cumulative global shipments of more than 20 million units, reflecting their continuously growing market acceptance.
Boasting technological prowess and rapid innovation, Chinese brands are reshaping long-held perceptions among consumers worldwide.
A foreign visitor tries out a stringless guitar at Yingyueli Block in Huishan Ancient Town, Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu province. (Photo/Pan Zhengguang)

items.title: AI innovation and testing center opens in Shenzhen
text: TUV Rheinland Greater China formally opened its InnoHub Shenzhen innovation center on Thursday as a dedicated AI-focused testing platform.

The facility features a full-chain "AI+" evaluation system that captures information about user experiences, software and hardware assessment, physical AI products and AIDC infrastructure, based on the demands of real-world users.

The center uses a three-tier evaluation framework. At the first layer, it verifies the performance, safety and reliability of artificial intelligence data center infrastructure. The middle layer assesses AI foundational models and software applications for functionality, security and long-term stability. The top tier accounts for human factors and performs multimodal tests for physical AI hardware including exoskeletons, robots and imaging devices.
The structure enables early-stage validation during product definition, prototyping and iteration, helping manufacturers spot risks and increase R&D efficiency, the company said.

Eight interconnected research zones form a closed-loop workflow from user research to a certification showcase. The Shenzhen hub complements the first InnoHub launched in Shanghai in July 2025. Shanghai focuses on smart cockpits and display and acoustic experiences, while Shenzhen specializes in AIDC infrastructure, large models and physical AI, forming a dual-city layout.
Jay Yang, global senior vice-president of TUV Rheinland Electrical, said as technology becomes smarter, evaluations must stay focused on people, real-world applications and user safety.

Jason Fu, vice-president of TUV Rheinland Greater China Electrical, said said that with InnoHub Shenzhen now open, the division will explore AI evaluation through its strong industrial ecosystem and real-world applications.

items.title: China's new environmental assessment rules ease burden on projects
text: China's revised catalog for the classified management of environmental impact assessments is expected to reduce the number of projects requiring formal environmental impact assessment approval by about 30,000 nationwide, or roughly 25 percent, by simplifying or easing requirements for certain types of projects, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment said.

The ministry recently released the 2027 edition of the catalog for classified management of environmental impact assessments for construction projects to further standardize and streamline environmental impact assessment procedures, ministry spokesman Pei Xiaofei said in a news conference on Friday.

The revision was made in line with the requirements of the Ecological and Environmental Code, he said. It adds greenhouse gas emissions as a basis for determining environmental impact assessment categories and gives greater consideration to coordinated reductions in pollution and carbon emissions in key industries.

The new catalog is also designed to support the development of new quality productive forces and improve services for projects that affect people's livelihoods, Pei noted. It optimizes environmental impact assessment management for advanced manufacturing sectors, including aerospace equipment and smart consumer devices, while simplifying environmental impact assessment requirements for certain livelihood-related projects, such as grain milling and bamboo and wood charcoal production.
Pei stressed, however, the revision maintains strict environmental access requirements for projects with high energy consumption and high emissions, as well as projects with major ecological impacts.

It also standardizes the environmental impact assessment classification of projects involving the co-firing of fuels in thermal power plants and strengthens environmental impact assessment management for large and medium-sized hubs for water resources management, the spokesman added.
The new catalog will come into force on Jan 1, Pei said.

items.title: Luanzhou shadow puppetry keeps 400-year tradition alive in Hebei
text: Inside a shadow-play workshop in the ancient city scenic area of Luanzhou in Tangshan, Hebei province, traditional shadow plays are staged as visitors stop to watch and photograph the performance.

Tangshan shadow puppetry, among China's first national-level intangible cultural heritage items, has a history of more than 400 years. Known as "donkey-hide shadow puppetry", it combines carving, painting, and sung storytelling.

The art has a complete role system divided into six categories. Its classic facial design features a straight nose, high and curved brows linked to slender eyes, a small mouth, and a pointed chin, making them easy to identify.
Crafting a qualified puppet requires multiple procedures, including soaking, scraping, and pasting the hide, selecting leather, carving, coloring, varnishing, and attaching rods.
Its singing is based on the local dialect, and its signature "pinched-throat" vocal method is the most distinctive feature separating Luanzhou shadow puppetry from other schools in China.

In recent years, Luanzhou has promoted cultural tourism integration and intangible heritage programs in schools, local authorities said. Local primary and secondary schools offer shadow-puppetry courses, with inheritors teaching young people carving, manipulation, and singing skills.

The ancient city's scenic area has built a shadow-play art workshop that regularly stages plays and sells cultural products, attracting tourists from across the country. Some international visitors have also experienced the art firsthand.
Other local heritage items, such as clay sculpture, are also being taught to enrich traditional culture classes for young people.

items.title: 'Space kitchen' upgrades menu as China's Tiangong welcomes first foreign astronaut
text: BEIJING -- A plate of freshly baked cakes was waiting for Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali as he entered China's Tiangong space station, offering a warm welcome to its first foreign crew member while highlighting upgrades to the "space kitchen," video released by the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) shows.

Ali and his two Chinese crewmates entered the Tiangong station on Wednesday afternoon, hours after the Shenzhou XXIV spacecraft lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center at 8:18 am (Beijing Time).

Shenzhou XXIII crew member Lai Ka-ying, the first astronaut from China's Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, presented a plate of small cakes fresh from the station's oven. "I just baked these space cupcakes to welcome you," she said with a smile.
Shenzhou XXIII mission commander Zhu Yangzhu added, "Baked today." Ali held the plate with both hands, leaned in to smell the cakes, and declared in Mandarin, "Very good!"

The heartwarming exchange offered an early glimpse of life aboard Tiangong during a period of joint operations involving six astronauts. Ali and two members of the Shenzhou XXIII crew are scheduled to return to Earth after the period of overlap.
Food will be an important part of Ali's adjustment to life in orbit, and how well the specially prepared meals suit his tastes and nutritional needs will be watched closely.

Preparations began well before launch. Soon after Ali and his fellow countryman Khurram Daud were selected as the final candidates for China's space mission training in April, the Astronaut Center of China (ACC) began developing the space food menu.

It reviewed and adapted items from the existing space food library to build a dedicated Pakistani food reserve of more than 100 items, developing seven specialty dishes in Pakistani flavors, including nihari beef and lamb korma.

"We designed the recipes on the basis of ensuring energy and nutrient standards are met, taking into account the need for light, easily digestible food during the early days in orbit, and then tailored them to their personal needs," said Chen Junli of the ACC.

"Pakistani people favor spices such as turmeric and curry, so we developed space foods like curry chickpeas and butter chicken that suit local tastes," Chen said. "The entire production line is a fully halal one."
Chen added the foods went through repeated tastings and iterative recipe optimization. "During the tastings, their feedback was positive."

The team also adjusted the menu based on their feedback. "In our initial design we wanted to include popular Pakistani spiced milk tea, but after they came to China, they found Chinese black tea and rice particularly tasty, and asked for more of both during the mission, so we took that into account in the menu design," Chen said.

The broader "space kitchen" upgrades are not tailored to any single crew member. Tiangong's food repertoire has expanded to nearly 200 varieties, and the rotating menu cycle has been extended to 10 days. With microwave ovens and baking equipment, crews can now enjoy hot meals within 20 minutes and fresh bread, vegetables and nuts prepared in orbit, according to the CMSA.

items.title: Beijing expands access to surgical robots through leasing
text: Beijing is expanding the use of surgical robots in hospitals through a pioneering financial leasing platform, with 16 robots already leased to 10 medical institutions and another 13 in the pipeline, a municipal health official said on Thursday.

The platform, the first of its kind in China, aims to lower the financial barriers for hospitals to acquire high-end medical equipment through what officials describe as "full life-cycle services", including installment-based rental payments, maintenance and upgrades, replacement guarantees, and flexible disposal arrangements.

Chen Hang, deputy director of the Beijing Health Commission, made the remarks at a news conference on the city's efforts to promote drug safety and high-quality development during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30) on Thursday.
"Medical surgical robots are an important example of innovative medical devices and a key strength of Beijing's high-end medical equipment sector," he said.

A total of 45 registration certificates for medical surgical robots have been approved in Beijing, the highest number among provincial-level regions nationwide, Chen said. The robots are used in a range of specialties, including orthopedics, neurosurgery, dentistry, laparoscopic surgery, and interventional procedures, with their applications gradually extending to ophthalmology, cardiovascular medicine, radiotherapy, and pediatrics.

By the end of the third quarter of 2026, municipal hospitals in Beijing had put 61 surgical robots into operation. Since 2024, the devices have assisted in more than 34,000 procedures, including over 13,700 in the first three quarters of this year, up 49 percent year-on-year, Chen said.

"Beijing will leverage its strengths in medical resources and technological innovation and continue to improve services across the entire chain, from research and development to application, so that more innovative surgical robots can enter hospitals, be used in clinical practice, and benefit more patients," he said.

On the industrial front, Beijing-made orthopedic surgical robots have reached more than 200 tertiary Grade A hospitals across all 31 provincial-level regions in China, assisting in more than 150,000 procedures. A domestically developed single-port laparoscopic surgical robot has also entered markets in Europe and the United States, Chen added.

items.title: 24 injured in Hong Kong boat accident
text: HONG KONG -- A boat hit hard objects in waters near Tsing Yi Oil Depot on Friday morning, injuring 24 people, the Hong Kong Police Force said on Friday.
Rescue has arrived at the scene, and the cause of the accident is under investigation.

items.title: SK Hynix hosts annual employee gathering in Wuxi
text: More than 4,000 employees of SK Hynix Wuxi gathered on Nov 24 for the company's 10th annual Happy Party, a day of food, performances, games and community activities at its employee residential compound in Wuxi National Hi-Tech District.

With more than 90 percent of its workforce coming from outside Wuxi, the South Korean semiconductor company has developed a range of facilities and services to support employees living away from home. Its residential compound currently accommodates more than 900 employees, offering furnished apartments as well as dining halls, a gym, a cinema, an internet cafe, a library and reading rooms.

Other support measures include shuttle bus services, dining options featuring both Chinese and South Korean food, and an on-site clinic. The company also provides regular health checkups, mental health support, and travel subsidies for employees visiting their families.

For Elena Cha, a South Korean employee who has been living in Wuxi for a year, settling into the city proved easier than expected. Colleagues helped her get acquainted with local life, taking her to explore Nanchang Street and sample Wuxi's local cuisine on weekends.
The city's welcoming atmosphere and the company's strong employee support services have helped her build a comfortable life here. "I now regard Wuxi as my second home," she said.

items.title: Still flying high
text: In 2023, Malaysian singer Vanessa Reynauld, born in the 2000s, came to public attention with her rendition of To Fly Away on The Voice of China. She later took part in the Chinese variety show Singer 2026 · Malaysia. Recently, she held her first solo concert at Blue Note in Beijing, once again performing the song that brought her to the spotlight.
Talking about her connection with China, the singer recalled how she grabbed a mic at a wedding and sang The Moon Represents My Heart when she was just 4.

Having been to China many times, she is impressed by Chinese singers' perfectionism and dedication. "They are always practicing. Chinese singers can really serve as role models, and I feel I should work harder to match their level."
She said she has experienced the affection and warmth of people in China and hopes to return more often to explore new experiences.

46th edition of global tech showcase opens with the inaugural GITEX SUMMIT on 7 December to shape the 2027 reset

Dubai, UAE: Dubai is set to become the epicentre of an intensifying global conversation on the future AI economy next month, as tech leaders, policymakers, investors and innovators from more than 120 countries fill 46 sold-out halls at the world’s largest and most international tech and AI event of the year.

items.title: Huawei Highlights Patent Licensing and Open Innovation at Seventh IP Forum
text: Huawei brought together global innovation and intellectual property (IP) experts and industry partners at its seventh Innovation and Intellectual Property Forum in Beijing on November 24, where it reported approximately US$800 million in patent licensing revenue for 2025 and agreements with 20 new licensees.

Held under the theme “Invent to Excel, Open to Empower,” the forum reaffirmed the role of openness in driving industry innovation and of IP protection in safeguarding it. Participants explored how sustained innovation can accelerate technological progress and how open collaboration can support industry development as AI reshapes the global economy.

“At Huawei, a patent represents more than a legal right. It represents an innovative achievement and a source of pride for the people behind it,” said Alan, Huawei’s vice president and chief intellectual property officer.

items.title: A Spanish Photographer in Shanghai: Capturing the Moments That Make a Family
text: For Spanish photographer Nuria Sánchez, family photography is about preserving the moments that matter most. Born in Málaga, on Spain's southern coast, she has made Shanghai her home for the past 11 years, building a practice focused on families, maternity and weddings.

Her path to photography began in childhood, led her through a career in human resources, and eventually brought her back to the work she loves. Today, she hopes to offer families in Shanghai a more natural, relaxed and spontaneous approach to photography – one that captures not just how a family looks, but the memories they make together.
Born in Málaga, on Spain's southern coast, Nuria Sánchez has made Shanghai her home for the past 11 years, building a practice focused on families, maternity and weddings. Andrea Martinez
Before we talk about business, would you please introduce yourself?

I don't remember exactly when my passion for photography began, but it must have been at a very young age. On the day of my First Communion, when I was nine, I received four cameras as gifts. It seems my relatives and friends had recognized my love of photography before I had fully realized it myself.

At 14, while still in secondary school, I began studying photography. I became the photographer for my friends, who enjoyed playing the role of models, and some of my pictures were even displayed in the school hallways. Later, I started accompanying other photographers to weddings, earning a little money while doing something I loved. I often preferred that to going out with my friends.

I eventually completed my studies in human resources and worked as a labor consultant. But I later changed the course of my life and pursued formal training as a higher technician in imaging. My first assignments were documentaries and exhibitions, followed by weddings.

It was after having my own children that I became interested in family photography. I wanted to keep them little forever and preserve those fleeting moments, because children grow up so quickly. Many of my wedding clients also had children or were expecting, and that's how I began working in maternity and family photography.
It was after having her own children that Nuria became interested in family photography. She wanted to keep them little forever and preserve those fleeting moments. Andrea Martinez
Why did you decide to strike out on your own to build up a business?

When I first arrived in China, I spent the first two years settling my family into our new life and getting to know the city, its culture and language. Once everything had fallen into place, however, my passion for photography drew me back to work, and I felt more eager than ever to pursue it in Shanghai.
Nuria captures an intimate moment of everyday family life on the streets of Shanghai. Courtesy of Nuria Sánchez
An expat family poses for a family portrait on the city's iconic riverfront. Courtesy of Nuria Sánchez

items.title: Chinese American Fields Medalist Calls for Math Collaboration in AI Age
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019334/Chinese American Fields Medalist Calls for Math Collaboration in AI Age
text: Arguing that artificial intelligence could help mathematicians solve difficult problems, Chinese American Fields Medal winner Shing-Tung Yau said humans still have a place in pushing mathematics to new heights.

“Mathematics is not in crisis. It will only get better,” Yau told Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper on Nov. 23, saying that much of the anxiety surrounding AI stemmed from an excessive focus on problem-solving rather than the broader pursuit of mathematical discovery.

Yau, the founding president of the Asian Mathematical Union, the first pan-Asian academic organization dedicated to mathematics, called for greater collaboration among mathematicians at the union’s launch ceremony on Tuesday at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. He added that rapid advances in AI offer Asian mathematicians a chance not only to catch up with their international peers but also to overtake them.

Over the past year, AI has made a series of remarkable breakthroughs in mathematics. In May, a model from American AI company OpenAI disproved the Erdős unit distance conjecture, a problem that had remained open for 80 years.

On Nov. 20, mathematician Levent Alpöge, working for American AI company Anthropic, unveiled a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’ most famous unsolved problems, developed with the help of the company’s AI system Claude. Mathematicians are now working to understand the reasoning behind the proof.

“In mathematics, it’s often only after we’ve repeatedly used a theorem over a long period of time that we know the proof is sound,” Yau explained to The Paper. He expects mathematicians to fully digest the proof of the Riemann hypothesis within five years.

“Whether the Riemann hypothesis was proved by a machine or the human brain, it’s an exciting achievement. To me, humanity’s goal is to pursue truth. As long as the truth can be discovered, there’s nothing wrong with using whatever tools we have to find it. Who gets the credit, I think, is secondary.”
Yau likened mathematical research to climbing mountains, saying AI could help mathematicians reach the first summit and open up paths to even greater heights.
“Climbing a mountain isn’t something one scholar can do alone,” he said. “Machines can speed up our collaboration by helping us bring together ideas from scientists around the world.”

In line with Yau’s emphasis on collaboration, the Asian Mathematical Union plans to recruit around 100 postdoctoral researchers annually: 50 selected by an academic committee, five each nominated by China, India, Russia, Japan, South Korea, and Iran, and 20 from other countries and regions. It also plans to regularly invite 25 senior mathematicians and 30 early career researchers from around the world to Hong Kong for research, academic exchanges, and training.
The union will focus on four areas: pure mathematics, applied mathematics, statistics, and AI.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Farmers’ Markets for the Masses: The Key to China’s Vibrant Local Food Culture
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019324/Farmers’ Markets for the Masses: The Key to China’s Vibrant Local Food Culture
text: Zhong Shuru has been working at a university in the southern Chinese city of Zhuhai for years. But she still regularly drives three hours north to the outskirts of Dongguan City just to stock up on chicken from her mother’s village.
This kind of commitment to fresh local produce is far from unusual in southern China’s Guangdong province, home to just over 125 million people and the birthplace of Cantonese cuisine.
“In Guangdong, we have a saying: Without chicken, there is no feast,” said Zhong, an associate professor of anthropology at Sun Yat-sen University.

The province consumes a whopping 800 million chickens a year, and locals pride themselves on their ability to taste the difference between “good chicken” — free-range birds raised for over 200 days — and the battery-farmed broilers used by most fast-food chains.
This passion for high-quality produce has shaped the region’s entire food supply chain, helping local networks survive even amid the rise of modern supermarket chains and online delivery services.
Even today, city dwellers across Guangdong can easily access fresh meat, seafood, fruits, and vegetables at relatively affordable prices via a dense web of neighborhood food markets.

For Zhong, these markets — often called “wet markets” in English — have long been a source of fascination: They are a relic of the pre-supermarket era, but also a potential antidote to industrial food production.

This point struck Zhong keenly when she began a Ph.D. at Texas A&M University. She quickly realized that such markets simply didn’t exist in much of the United States — unless you count expensive farmers’ markets.
During her time in Texas, Zhong found herself surviving mostly on pizza and pasta dishes to save time — a habit that added “about 10 kilograms” to her weight, she recalled.
That was when she decided to launch a research project into China’s food markets, aiming to understand the role they played in feeding the country.

In the summer of 2016, she began a work placement at a market stall selling Spanish mackerel in China’s southern province of Hainan, where she spent over a year tracing the fish’s journey from the South China Sea to dinner tables across the tropical island.
Over the following decade, she would visit more than 200 markets all over China, writing books including 2025’s “Sustainable Food Consumption in China.”
At the core of her research lies a burning question: Are local markets destined to decline in an era that prizes convenience, or could they help promote a resurgence in sustainable eating habits?

But first, it’s necessary to clear up a few common misconceptions. For years, the term “wet market” has fueled all sorts of prejudices in the English-speaking world, where negative stereotypes about Chinese eating habits have a long history.
Zhong specifically recalls a member of her Ph.D. committee in Texas frowning as she introduced her research subject. “What are wet markets?” the person asked. “Sounds disgusting.”

items.title: Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019331/Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
text: Amid nationwide classroom phone bans, “paper short dramas,” half-meter-long printouts of scenes from short dramas folded into the shape of a smartphone, have recently surged in popularity among Chinese primary school students.

“The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” “Reborn as the Heiress of a Tycoon,” and “The School Bully Forces Me to Date Him” are just a few examples of the stories now stocked by school-adjacent stores and e-commerce platforms, selling for as little as 1 yuan ($0.14), domestic media reported Monday.

In 2021, China’s Ministry of Education issued a notice stating that primary and secondary school students should not bring phones into the classroom, and any phone brought to school must be kept by the school. The ministry tightened this in 2025, banning phones and other electronic devices in school classrooms as part of a student mental health initiative.
Paper short dramas’ accordion-style design allow them to be easily concealed and taken into school. They typically contain scenes from multiple episodes, pairing screenshots with written dialogue.

Despite often containing adult, vulgar, and violent content — in “The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” for instance, a female character sleeps with a legendary CEO and becomes the envy of her peers — paper short dramas are marketed as toys, with some packaging citing toy-safety standards that are outdated or inapplicable to a paper booklet.
This marketing tactic allows sellers, who have not obtained permission from short drama producers to reproduce or distribute the content, to dodge copyright laws.
China’s short drama users reportedly reached nearly 664 million as of December last year. Industry estimates put the potential lost output value due to piracy at as high as 20 billion yuan.

In interviews with domestic media, some parents also reported concerns about the adult content in paper short dramas being available to children with no prior screening, saying that such stories might negatively impact their children’s values.

A hashtag related to paper short dramas on microblogging platform Weibo had garnered over 170 million views as of Thursday. Many commenters called the idea creative, terming it a “new kind of comic strip,” while others criticized it for exposing minors to harmful content.
“Products like this need tight control. Don’t let them poison kids,” one user wrote.
(Header image: A box of different paper short dramas, each shaped like a smartphone. From Weibo)

items.title: The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
text: Zhong Weiting’s wife recently bought him a pair of trousers with four front pockets. They’re for the little metal objects he carries around — things that spin, slide, click, or flip open, some made from titanium and costing thousands of yuan.
Each day, he picks a few from a plastic organizer originally bought for socks. He plays with them in elevators, in his car, and at his desk, switching to quieter models when other people are around.

For Zhong, 32, they help relieve stress and keep his restless hands occupied. “I like the sounds they make, and knowing exactly how they’ll respond gives me a sense of certainty,” he tells Sixth Tone. “I feel a kind of electric tingling in my fingertips.”

For all their elaborate mechanisms, they’re just toys to fiddle with. And Zhong, an export salesman in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen who began collecting only in November 2025, already owns 25, including one he bought this month for 2,199 yuan ($330).

Across China, the toys have found a growing following under the name EDC, short for “everyday carry,” a term borrowed from an online subculture centered on practical gear such as pocketknives and flashlights. On social media, they’re also dubbed “cyber walnuts,” after the traditional Chinese pastime of rolling a pair of walnuts in the hand.

Among the most popular designs are sliders, known in China as “push cards,” whose metal plates produce a series of tactile clicks as they slide against each other. Some toys mimic the motion of revealing a playing card or recreate the sharp tap of a telegraph key, with adjustable resistance and sound on more elaborate models.

Basic models sell for less than 100 yuan, while stainless steel versions typically cost 300 to 500 yuan. Limited editions made from rarer metals or featuring elaborate designs can run into the thousands.
Between July 2025 and June 2026, online sales of EDC toys tracked by consulting firm Meritco Databank rose 55.5% to more than 45 million yuan, with nearly 500,000 toys sold, up 78% year on year.

The vast majority of the trade, however, still takes place within collector circles. While a few large brands sell openly on popular e-commerce platforms, smaller makers rely on private groups on Chinese super app WeChat to announce new releases, sometimes limited to just a few dozen pieces.

At an EDC exhibition in Beijing in October, organizer Fu Chunjun told domestic media that the community has a name for its growing obsession: the “men’s version of Pop Mart,” the Chinese collectible-toy company known for its blind boxes.
But when Zhong shows his latest purchases to friends, few understand the appeal. “They think, why should a plastic or stainless steel gadget sell for 500 yuan?” he says.
To buy a toy from one vendor at Shanghai’s EDC exhibition in April, Guo Songhao first had to draw one of two jokers from a deck of 21 playing cards.

He drew the big joker, securing a limited-edition knuckle roller, a small metal toy designed to be rolled and flipped between the fingers. “My luck was pretty good that day,” the 25-year-old Shanghai-based engineer tells Sixth Tone.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
text: A Shanghai university is now giving each student and staff member up to 100 million AI tokens a week, saying that it hopes to make tokens a standard teaching resource equal to books, lab equipment, and databases.

University members may use the tokens to access a range of AI models and tools after signing in to the university website with their campus ID, as announced by Shanghai University of Finance and Economics’ (SUFE) official WeChat account on Nov. 21.
Tokens are the smallest pieces of information that AI models can process. Students can use them to debug code, clean data, conduct research, and even build their own AI agents.

China’s daily token consumption hit roughly 500 trillion in June, nearly four times that of December 2025. State-owned telecommunications carriers now sell token plans to consumers, with China Telecom’s cheapest plan costing 9.9 yuan ($1.50) a month for 10 million tokens — a 10th of SUFE’s weekly, per-person limit.
SUFE is the latest Chinese university to provide computing power and free token quotas to students and staff as a public resource, a trend that began earlier this fall.

Starting this September in Beijing, Tsinghua University began offering each student and staff member 1,000 yuan in “computing vouchers,” while Peking University offers a year of free access to Qoder, a cross-LLM AI coding assistant, and 3,000 credits a month. In the central Hunan province, Hunan University students receive 2 million tokens a day. Shanghai’s Tongji University also launched its own plan in October, giving students and faculty 100 million tokens a week.

“In the past, when you’d say a school had good infrastructure, you’d be referring to its gym and library,” Xue Lan, dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, told domestic media. “Going forward, computing platforms, LLM data centers, and high-powered internet may be the important infrastructure of schools in the future.”

However, education researchers also report concerns that access to free tokens may fuel “idle teaching,” where teachers create assignments using AI and students submit AI-generated answers, creating a loop in which the work is completed but no real learning takes place.

“Measuring the value of token use is not about how many tokens are actually consumed but what kind of learning they advance in students,” Zhang Duanhong, director of the Center for Educational Policy Research at Tongji University, told domestic media.

items.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
text: “Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.
“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.
“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.
(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

items.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
text: Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.
In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
text: Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.
The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.
Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.

Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang
text: Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang       Andy Lin, Mackenzie Hawkins and Kari Lindberg   Fri, November 27, 2026 at 4:45 AM MST 8 min read                                    NVDA                                (Bloomberg) -- A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.'s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker.
SAP Weighs Cutting at Least 10,000 Roles in AI Restructure
Trump Calls GDP Numbers 'Fake,' Demands Probe After Revision
South Africa Sentences Russia Army Recruit as Ukraine Urges Action
Nvidia Rehires Huang in Stunning Reversal After Trump Push
Billions in Data Center Deals Grind to Halt After Chip Curbs

The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia's most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News.

A second firm Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based parent, described a GB200 server — which also relies on Blackwell chips — at the facility. That description was provided in documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency.

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license.

President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge.

Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company's products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars.

It's unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site — described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers. By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology Co., which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks. The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company.

Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
text: Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that the DPP has not held for nearly three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Chinese chip stocks notch biggest ever one-day gains as Beijing signals broader market support
text: Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.

The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT, Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.

The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.

Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.

By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.

That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
